recent_posts.title: Comparing the Z80 and 6502 to Their Relatives
recent_posts.summary: A deep-dive comparison of classic 8-bit and 16-bit CPU architectures: the Intel 8080, Z80, 8086, Motorola 6800, 6809, and MOS 6502. The post traces the lineage and design philosophy of each chip, highlighting key differences in register sets, memory addressing modes, stack capabilities, and instruction encoding. It also revisits earlier assembly programming maxims for the 6502 and Z80, evaluating which advice still holds and adding new insights — notably that Z80 code is often faster when it's also valid 8080 code. Toolchain recommendations (NASM, Pasmo, WLA-DX, asm6809) are included for each architecture family.

recent_posts.title: Reconnecting with retro gaming and why old games still spark joy
recent_posts.summary: A nostalgic personal essay about reconnecting with retro gaming culture — touching a ZX Spectrum for the first time in decades, visiting a retro game store, and attending a video games show. The author reflects on how physical games created tangible memories and social bonds that modern digital gaming lacks, and how retro gaming communities still spark genuine human connection decades later.

recent_posts.title: Using a 1978 terminal in 2026 (DEC VT-100)
recent_posts.summary: A developer bought a 1978 DEC VT-100 terminal and attempted to use it as their main terminal in 2026, motivated by building a modern coding agent for the terminal. The experiment revealed three main compatibility challenges: flow control issues (requiring a Linux VM since macOS dropped support), slow 9600 baud speed requiring differential rendering to minimize redraws, and escape sequence incompatibilities including Unicode and OSC sequences that required adding ASCII-only and legacy modes. Despite these hurdles, the VT-100 was made functional for vim and the custom app, and the exercise surfaced real-world compatibility improvements that later benefited enterprise customers with non-Unicode terminals.

recent_posts.title: Commodore 64 Ultimate Line-Up Expands with C64C Edition Later this Year
recent_posts.summary: Commodore has announced the Commodore 64C Ultimate, a slimline FPGA-based recreation of the 1986-era C64C computer, now available for pre-order with shipping expected in late 2026. To maximize authenticity, Commodore reacquired the original injection molds used to manufacture the C64C plastic housing 40 years ago, including their original production imperfections. Three editions are planned: Basic Beige ($299.99), Starlight Edition ($349.99) with LED lighting, and Founder's Edition ($499.99) with gold-plated accents. The hardware offers cycle-accurate Commodore 64 performance and comes bundled with games, demos, and a spiral-bound user guide.

recent_posts.title: Restoring a rare Commodore 900 prototype through reverse engineering
recent_posts.summary: A FOSDEM 2025 talk about restoring a rare Commodore C900 prototype — a 1984 budget Unix workstation based on the Zilog Z8000 processor that was canceled when Commodore acquired Amiga. The speaker details the process of bringing the machine back to life, including disassembling the Z8000 BIOS, reverse-engineering the keyboard interface, and solving a hard disk low-level format mystery. The effort eventually helped two other Commodore 900 owners restore their machines as well.

recent_posts.title: Continuing the story of early DOS development
recent_posts.summary: Microsoft is continuing its effort to preserve early DOS history by releasing the earliest DOS source code discovered to date, on the 45th anniversary of 86-DOS 1.00. A team of historians led by Yufeng Gao and Rich Cini located, scanned, and transcribed assembler listings from Tim Paterson, the original author of DOS. The materials include sources to the 86-DOS 1.00 kernel, PC-DOS 1.00 development snapshots, and utilities like CHKDSK. These listings function like a printed commit history, showing how features were implemented and bugs fixed. The code is licensed under MIT and hosted at DOS-History/Paterson-Listings on GitHub. Physical artifacts will also be donated to the Interim Computer Museum.

recent_posts.title: Retro Repro Wiki
recent_posts.summary: retrorepro.wiki is a community wiki cataloguing modern reproduction parts for vintage computers, including replica PCBs, replacement cases, and re-manufactured chips. It covers systems like Macintosh, Apple II, Amiga, Commodore 64/128, IBM PC/XT/AT, Atari 8-bit and ST, and related hardware. The wiki focuses exclusively on reproduction and replacement parts — not original hardware documentation — helping enthusiasts find what has been reproduced and where to source it.

recent_posts.title: Inside the Atari 1200XL
recent_posts.summary: A hands-on look inside a non-working Atari 1200XL acquired from a Facebook Marketplace deal. The post covers the machine's unique keyboard layout with dedicated function keys (F1-F4), the motherboard's key chips including the MOS 6502C CPU, GTIA, ANTIC, POKEY, and PIA, as well as the cartridge port, joystick ports, and rear I/O. The author notes the 1200XL lacks built-in BASIC (like the 400 and 800), uses the same power supply as the Atari 800, and plans to use the Field Service manual to diagnose the no-video fault as a future repair project.

recent_posts.title: TEMPEST vs TEMPEST
recent_posts.summary: A free book-length deep dive into the source code and implementation details of two classic arcade games: Dave Theurer's Tempest (1981) and Jeff Minter's Tempest 2000 (1994). The book explores how game mechanics are implemented at the assembly level, covering both 6502 (Tempest) and 68K Motorola (Tempest 2000) assembler code. Available as a free PDF download, with a high-resolution version also available.

recent_posts.title: Detecting DOSBox from within the Box
recent_posts.summary: A deep technical exploration of how to detect DOSBox from within the emulator itself. The author discovers that DOSBox implements a custom, undocumented x86 opcode (FE /7) used internally for its callback mechanism in virtual programs like MOUNT.COM. By setting up an INT 06h (#UD) exception handler, code can test whether this secret instruction executes silently (DOSBox) or triggers an undefined opcode exception (real hardware or other emulators). The post also covers x86 instruction encoding details, a bug discovered in 86Box/PCem where FE group opcodes were mishandled, and briefly touches on detection methods for NTVDM, Win9x DOS prompt, and DOSEMU.
